- When sentiment is positive (≥0.5) and forecast is rising sharply, reduce overshoot by 5–10% to avoid overreacting to short-term momentum.  
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.2) and forecast is falling, avoid excessive downward bias — adjust downward only if recent price action confirms trend, not just sentiment.  
- After a spike in price (e.g., >85), model tends to overcorrect — reduce forecast peak by 5–10% and slow decay to allow for mean reversion.  
- If sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish cycles (e.g., 0.8 → 0.2 → 0.8), model often misaligns with sentiment — adjust forecast to match sentiment’s recent direction, not just historical mean.  
- For 30-day horizon, model often underestimates late-period volatility — increase forecast tail risk (last 5–7 days) by 3–5% if sentiment is volatile or recent price action is erratic.  
- If sentiment is consistently low (≤0.2) over 3–5 days, model tends to overcorrect downward — increase forecast slightly to avoid “sentiment-induced sell-off” bias.
